results.body:
The former President of the East Aurora, Ill. School District 131 Board of Education directed $1.3 million to a company for which she was the Chief Financial Officer as a kickback or bribe in exchange for taking acts in her capacity as President to approve the purchase of air purifiers from a school district vendor, according to an indictment returned Tuesday in federal court in Chicago.

The indictment accuses ANNETTE JOHNSON of steering District 131 to purchase air purifiers from the vendor for approximately $2.7 million in 2021 and voting in favor of the purchase.  District 131 paid for the air purifiers using Covid-era federal grant funds, the indictment states.  Unbeknownst to the other District 131 board members, Johnson and the vendor had agreed that the vendor would pay a company owned by Johnson’s boyfriend—and where Johnson worked as the Chief Financial Officer—more than $1 million of the proceeds of the sale, the indictment states.  Within days of a Board vote, in which Johnson participated and approved payment from District 131 to the vendor, the vendor mailed a $1.3 million check, labeled “commission,” to the company where Johnson was the Chief Financial Officer, the indictment states. 

Johnson was the President of the District 131 Board of Education at the time of the alleged fraud scheme, and she currently remains a member of the Board.

The indictment charges Johnson, 63, of Aurora, Ill., with two counts of honest services mail fraud and one count of honest services wire fraud, each of which is punishable by up to 20 years in federal prison.  Arraignment in federal court in Chicago has not yet been scheduled. 

The indictment was announced by Andrew S. Boutros, United States Attorney for the Northern District of Illinois; Scott Wingle, Acting Special Agent-in-Charge of the U.S. Department of Education Office of Inspector General’s Central Regional Office; and Ryan Whalen, Special Agent-in-Charge of the Chicago Field Office of the FBI.  The government is represented by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Edward A. Liva, Jr. and Adam Rosenbloom.

The public is reminded that an indictment is not evidence of guilt.  The defendant is presumed innocent and entitled to a fair trial at which the government has the burden of proving guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.  If convicted, the Court must impose reasonable sentences under federal statutes and the advisory U.S. Sentencing Guidelines.

The Justice Department’s Antitrust Division provided the following statement on the closing of its investigations into two transactions that presented competition issues in local asphalt markets: (1) the acquisition of Suit-Kote Corporation by Colas Inc., a subsidiary of Bouygues S.A.; and (2) the acquisition of Arcosa Inc. by CRH plc.

Colas/Suit-Kote. In August 2025, Bouygues (Colas) announced its intention to acquire Suit-Kote. Both companies offer asphalt pavement products and services to commercial and government customers in New York and Pennsylvania. The Antitrust Division opened an investigation into the acquisition and issued Second Requests to the parties in October 2025.

The Division investigated the transaction extensively, identified only discrete geographic areas in New York and Pennsylvania where the merger would reduce the number of asphalt suppliers, and referred the matter to those states. The parties offered the Division a divestiture of certain facilities serving those areas. To permit the states to engage with the parties regarding potential remedies, the Division fully referred the matter to the states.

The parties and states subsequently agreed to a settlement that includes divestiture of four facilities in New York and Pennsylvania. See Investigation of Colas Inc. & Suit-Kote Corp., Assurance No. 26-065 (N.Y. Att’y Gen. Oct. 13, 2026); Pennsylvania v. Colas Inc., No. 3:26-cv-1979 (W.D. Pa. filed Oct. 13, 2026).

CRH/Arcosa. In June 2026, CRH, an Irish building materials provider, announced its intention to acquire Arcosa, a U.S.-based infrastructure-related materials provider, for approximately $8.5 billion. The Antitrust Division opened an investigation into the acquisition.

The Division’s preliminary investigation identified and narrowed potential competition concerns to those in a local market for the sale of hot-mix asphalt in a region within New Jersey. Accordingly, as in Colas/Suit-Kote, the Division referred the matter to the New Jersey Attorney General. The Division kept open its investigation without issuing a Second Request to monitor progress with New Jersey and to facilitate expeditious resolution of any local competitive concerns.

Following that referral, the parties agreed with the New Jersey Attorney General to divest certain facilities in New Jersey. See Davenport v. CRH plc, No. 3:26-cv-13625 (D.N.J. filed Oct. 20, 2026).

In both matters, the Division commends the states and parties for reaching agreement to resolve the states’ concerns about competition in their local markets.[1] The Division continues to prioritize efficient use of federal enforcement resources and the complementary support of State Attorney General enforcement partners in local matters.

[1] The Division takes no position on the terms of the settlements.

ALEXANDRIA — On October 23, 2026, United States District Judge Jerry Edwards, Jr., sentenced three defendants on federal firearms and ammunition charges.

Judge Edwards sentenced Robert “Snoop” Taylor, 32, of Alexandria, to 63 months in federal prison for Possession of a Firearm by a Convicted Felon, followed by two years of supervised release.  Taylor previously pled guilty to the charge on July 8, 2026.

Judge Edwards also sentenced Kevin Guthrie, Jr., 42, of Alexandria, to 46 months in federal prison for Possession of Ammunition by a Convicted Felon, followed by two years of supervised release.  Guthrie also pled guilty to the charge on July 8, 2026.   

Finally, Judge Edwards sentenced Qwadarius L. Guthrie, 26, of Alexandria, to 46 months in federal prison for Possession of a Firearm by a Convicted Felon, followed by two years of supervised release. He pled guilty on June 29, 2026.

TAYLOR 
According to court documents, Alexandria Police Department (APD) officers responded to a November 2025 shooting in which the victim and a witness identified Taylor as the individual who fired a black semiautomatic pistol. The next day, officers located Taylor walking on a local street and arrested him. During the arrest, officers recovered a Taurus G3 9mm pistol from his pocket. Taylor admitted possessing the firearm. Taylor had prior felony convictions for burglary and battery and acknowledged he was aware it was illegal for him to possess a firearm.

This case was investigated by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) with assistance from APD. It was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Lauren S. Sarver with assistance from Paralegal Specialist Joanne Henry-Mills.

KEVIN GUTHRIE, JR. 
According to court documents, during a mandatory home visit on October 14, 2025, Louisiana Probation and Parole officers (LPP) assisted by APD, searched Guthrie’s residence. Inside his bedroom, officers found a drum magazine loaded with sixty rounds of 5.56 ammunition, two Glock .40-caliber magazines loaded with twelve rounds each, and seventeen rounds of 6.5 Creedmoor ammunition.  Guthrie was on probation for a prior felony conviction and prohibited from possessing ammunition.  

This case was investigated by the ATF with assistance from APD and LPP.  It was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Lauren S. Sarver with assistance from Paralegal Specialist Joanne Henry-Mills.

QWADARIUS L. GUTHRIE 
According to court documents, on October 14, 2025, an APD officer encountered Guthrie seated alone in a vehicle parked near a business. Items associated with illegal drug use were visible inside the vehicle. Guthrie consented to searches of his person and vehicle, at which time officers located a Smith & Wesson pistol and marijuana in the trunk. Guthrie admitted the firearm and narcotics were his. Guthrie had previous felony convictions, including aggravated second-degree battery and possession of Schedule I controlled substances, and acknowledged he was aware of his status as a convicted felon.

This case was investigated by ATF with assistance from APD. It was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney J. Daniel Siefker with assistance from Paralegal Specialist Denise Duhon.

U.S. Attorney Zachary A. Keller for the Western District of Louisiana made the announcement.

These cases were prosecuted as part of Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN), the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities. Learn more at www.justice.gov/psn.

You may find a copy of this press release (and any updates) on the website of the United States Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Louisiana at www.justice.gov/usao-wdla.

Related court documents and information may be found on the website of the District Court for the Western District of Louisiana at www.lawd.uscourts.gov or at https://www.lawd.uscourts.gov/cmecf-pacer under the following case numbers:

Taylor – 1:26-cr-00110 
Kevin Guthrie – 1:26-cr-00111

WILMINGTON, N.C. – Daquan Copeland, 35, of Houston, TX and Esless White Sr., 51, of Jamaica, NY, pleaded guilty in federal court to Conspiracy to Commit Mail Fraud by engaging in a scheme with others to defraud the federal government of more than $187,000. Each faces up to 30 years in federal prison and a fine of up to one million dollars when they are sentenced later this year.

“These two leeches bled dollars from federal programs designed to help those in need. Now they sit and wait for the gavel of justice to hammer down their sentence,” said U.S. Attorney, Ellis Boyle. “Anyone who defrauds any of our taxpayer programs will be held accountable. Know this, we are watching, we will catch you, we will prosecute you. Crime Doesn’t Pay! Cheaters. Never. Win.”

Copeland and White applied for emergency rental assistance through the North Carolina Housing Opportunities and Prevention of Evictions (NC HOPE) program. As part of their scheme, they and others submitted fake tenant leases for several properties in Lenoir County to support their applications. Between November 2020 and December 2021, Copeland, White, and others submitted 23 fraudulent applications and stole more than $187,000 in government housing funds for their personal use.

 On March 27, 2020, Congress passed the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security (CARES) Act to provide emergency financial support to millions of Americans affected by the economic fallout of the COVID‑19 pandemic. As part of this relief, the CARES Act authorized $5 billion for Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) programs, giving states and local governments flexible federal funding to prevent, prepare for, and respond to the pandemic. The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) manages the CDBG program, which supports economic and community development and provides long‑term recovery funding to states and localities after disasters and emergencies.

“Daquan Copeland and Esless White participated in a conspiracy that diverted more than $180,000 in limited taxpayer funds for their own enrichment, depriving a pandemic relief program of resources intended to help people struggling to remain in their homes," said Special Agent in Charge Jerome Winkle with the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), Office of Inspector General (OIG).  “This was not a victimless crime.  Every dollar stolen was a dollar unavailable to help someone pay rent during an unprecedented national crisis.  HUD OIG remains committed to working alongside our prosecutorial and law enforcement partners to aggressively pursue those who exploit HUD programs for personal gain.”

"This case reflects the strength of our partnerships with the USAO-EDNC and HUD-OIG in fighting fraud, waste and abuse that hurts our most vulnerable citizens,” said NCSBI Director, Chip Hawley. “Thanks also to USMS and the Kinston Police Department for their help. We will continue to aggressively target those who steal from hardworking taxpayers."

 The State of North Carolina’s Office of Recovery and Resiliency, a division of the North Carolina Department of Public Safety under then – Governor Roy Cooper, gave away federal funds made available in the CARES Act to supposedly North Carolina renters to ostensibly let them stay in their homes during COVID-19 by preventing evictions and the loss of utility services.  The NC HOPE program utilized an initial $51.5 million allocation of CDBG funds from the CARES Act to provide housing and utility assistance.  The State of North Carolina also received CRF funds from the CARES Act, of which $66 million was allocated to pay administrative costs associated with the NC HOPE program. 

Ellis Boyle, U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of North Carolina made the announcement after Chief U.S. District Judge Richard E. Myers II accepted the plea. The United States Department of Housing and Urban Development – OIG, and the SBI are investigating the case.

A copy of this press release is located on our website. Related court documents and information can be found on the website of the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of North Carolina or on PACER by searching for Case No. 4:26-CR-14-M.
results.title: Fraud Scheme Exposed: 2 From Texas and New York Stole COVID Federal Housing Funds from NC HOPE Program

MIAMI – A St. Augustine man pleaded guilty to attempted sex trafficking of a child after agreeing to pay $120 to have sex with someone he believed was a 15-year-old girl and traveling to Palm Beach County to meet with her.

According to court records and evidence presented at trial, Shannon Jermaine Hollingsworth, 45, of St. Augustine, arranged to pay $120 to have sex with a person he believed was 15 years old. He then traveled to the agreed-upon location, where he arrived carrying cash and a condom.

Following his arrest, Hollingsworth claimed that he had traveled to the location to rescue the child and was “just about to call” the police.  

“Shannon Jermaine Hollingsworth came to Palm Beach County with cash and a condom, intending to pay for sex with someone he believed was a 15-year-old child,” said U.S. Attorney Jason A. Reding Quiñones for the Southern District of Florida. “When confronted, he claimed he was there to rescue her. But that claim could not withstand the evidence presented by our prosecutors, and on the second day of trial, he pleaded guilty. We will continue working shoulder to shoulder with our law enforcement partners to protect children and bring those who seek to exploit them to justice.”

Hollingsworth faces a mandatory minimum sentence of 10 years and up to life in federal prison. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

U.S. Attorney Reding Quiñones and Special Agent in Charge José R. Figueroa of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Miami made the announcement.

HSI Miami and the Palm Beach County Sheriff’s Office are investigating the case, with assistance from the West Palm Beach Police Department. 

Assistant U.S. Attorneys Justin Chapman and Daniel Funk are prosecuting the case.

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and CEOS, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to better locate, apprehend, and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, visit www.justice.gov/psc.

Related court documents and information may be found on the website of the District Court for the Southern District of Florida at www.flsd.uscourts.gov or at http://pacer.flsd.uscourts.gov, under case number 26-cr-80031.
